packages.title: ActionSheet
packages.summary: Show the system's own action sheet and find out which option the user picked.
packages.description: Presents a list of choices in the platform's native action sheet or bottom sheet and gives you back the value of the row the user chose, or nothing if they dismissed it. You supply the rows, the title and the message, and mark destructive choices so the system styles them.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when the user must choose one action from a short list, such as share, edit or delete for an item. For choosing a value in a form or a long list, use a picker or list screen instead.
packages.nativeValue: The sheet looks and behaves like the rest of the phone, with the right styling for destructive rows and the system's own dismiss gestures.

actions.name: show
actions.description: Shows the action sheet and waits. You get the value of the chosen row, or nothing when the user dismissed it.
actions.whenNotToUse: Do not use it for long lists or for choices that need typed input.

params.name: items
params.description: The rows to show, top to bottom, each with a label, a value and an optional role; leave it out and nothing is shown, the call resolves null.

params.name: message
params.description: A line of explanation under the title; leave it out for none.

params.name: title
params.description: The title line shown at the top of the sheet; leave it out for none.

examples.title: picking a row resolves its value
a missing items list resolves null without presenting

events.name: select
events.description: The user picked a row or dismissed the sheet. Dismissing sends no value.

payload.name: value
payload.description: The value of the row the user chose, or empty when they dismissed the sheet.

packages.title: Adjust
packages.summary: Find out which ad or campaign brought each install, using Adjust.
packages.description: Works with the Product analytics package: on first launch it asks Adjust where the install came from and passes the campaign details on to your analytics destination. Needs an Adjust account and your app token. You also pick sandbox or production. Phones only.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when you buy installs through Adjust and want each install tied to its campaign in your analytics. Skip it if you do not use Adjust, or if probabilistic matching is on for your Adjust app and you cannot declare deterministic-only matching, because no install is attributed then.

actions.name: install
actions.description: Asks Adjust where this install came from and returns the campaign details. Growth calls it once on first launch; it returns nothing for organic installs, rejected installs, or when you have not declared deterministic-only matching.

params.name: token
params.description: Not used by this action. It is accepted so every attribution source shares one call shape.

result.name: adGroup
result.description: The ad group inside the campaign that brought the install.

result.name: campaign
result.description: The name of the campaign that brought the install.

result.name: creative
result.description: The ad creative that the person tapped before installing.

result.name: method
result.description: How the install was matched. It is always deterministic, which means the install was matched to a specific device.

result.name: referrer
result.description: The ad network that brought the install, as Adjust reports it.

result.name: source
result.description: The attribution source that answered. It is always adjust.

packages.title: Google AdMob
packages.summary: Show banner, interstitial, rewarded and native ads from Google AdMob.
packages.description: Shows full-screen and rewarded ads on demand and places banner and native ads inside your screens, with the consent prompt for users who need it. You decide where and when ads appear. Needs a Google AdMob account, your AdMob App ID and an ad unit ID for each ad type you use.

packages.title: AgeAssurance
packages.summary: Ask the phone's operating system for the user's age range.
packages.description: Uses Apple's Declared Age Range on iOS and Google's Play Age Signals on Android to learn which age band the user is in, without asking for a birthdate. Both give the same answer shape, with a yes, no or unknown result for each age you test. It asks the system to show its own prompt. You write what your app does for each age group.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when you must treat under-age users differently, for example to show or hide adult content. Check for yes with a strict true test, because unknown is not the same as no. If the system cannot answer, ask for a birthdate yourself.
packages.nativeValue: The age comes from the operating system's own family and account data, which a web page cannot see.

actions.name: check
actions.description: Asks the system for the user's age band and tells whether the user is at least each age you list; the system may show a prompt.
actions.whenToUse: Call it once when you need the answer, then read the result from the last action or the saved status.

packages.title: Airbridge
packages.summary: Attribute installs to ad campaigns and open deep links with Airbridge.
packages.description: Starts the Airbridge SDK at launch, reports which campaign led to an install and handles deferred deep links, so a new user lands on the right screen. It can wait for the iOS tracking permission decision. Needs an Airbridge account, your app name and app SDK token. Phones only.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it when you buy ads and want to know which campaign produced each install and sale, and to send new users to the right screen through deferred deep links. Skip it if you do not use Airbridge.
packages.nativeValue: The native SDK reads install referrers and iOS attribution data that a web page cannot, and it survives the store install.

packages.title: Alarms and timers
packages.summary: Set alarms and timers that ring even when the phone is on silent or locked.
packages.description: Schedule one-time or repeating alarms and countdown timers, with pause, snooze and stop. On iOS 26 they ring through Silent mode and Focus and show on the Lock Screen, and on Android they take over the lock screen. Good for clock, wake-up, cooking and reminder apps. Asks the user for permission.
packages.whenToUse: Use it to build alarm clocks, timers, wake-up and reminder features that must ring even when the phone is locked or silent. For a plain reminder text, a notification is enough.
packages.nativeValue: On iOS 26 alarms ring through Silent mode and Focus and show on the Lock Screen, and Android takes over the lock screen, which a web page cannot do.

actions.name: schedule
actions.description: Sets an alarm for a date and time, or for a clock time that repeats on chosen weekdays, and returns the alarm with its next ring time.
actions.whenToUse: Use it for wake-up and reminder alarms.
actions.whenNotToUse: Use timer for a countdown.

params.name: at
params.description: A one-time date and time as ISO 8601 text with a zone. Give exactly one of at and time.

params.description: Your own payload, handed back on the alarm and on every event it fires.

params.description: Your own id for the alarm, 1 to 64 letters, digits, underscore, dot or hyphen. One is generated when left out, and reusing an id replaces that alarm.

params.description: The name of your own activity component drawn as this alarm's Live Activity on iOS and its notification on Android. Without it a built-in card is used.

params.description: Set false to never show a permission dialog; a call that would have asked then fails with permission_denied.

params.description: A clock time as HH:MM on the 24 hour clock, in the device's time zone when it rings. Give exactly one of at and time.

params.name: tint
params.description: An accent colour as #RRGGBB for the alert, notification or card.

params.description: The title shown on the alert, the Lock Screen and the notification; defaults to Alarm, or Timer for timers.

actions.name: timer
actions.description: Starts a countdown that rings when it reaches zero, and returns the running timer.
actions.whenToUse: Use it for cooking, workout and focus timers.

params.name: data
params.description: Your own payload, handed back on the alarm and on every event it fires.

params.name: duration
params.description: How long the timer runs, as whole seconds from 1 to 86400.

params.name: id
params.description: Your own id for the alarm, 1 to 64 letters, digits, underscore, dot or hyphen. One is generated when left out, and reusing an id replaces that alarm.

params.name: layout
params.description: The name of your own activity component drawn as this alarm's Live Activity on iOS and its notification on Android. Without it a built-in card is used.

params.name: mission
params.description: The name of your own component that the person must complete to end the ring. It receives the alarm id as alarmId and ends the alarm by calling stop.

params.name: missionLabel
params.description: The label of the mission button, up to 40 characters; defaults to Start mission.

params.name: prompt
params.description: Set false to never show a permission dialog; a call that would have asked then fails with permission_denied.

params.name: rearm
params.description: Seconds after which a mission alarm that was silenced before its mission rings again, 0 or 10 to 3600, default 30. Needs mission.

params.name: snooze
params.description: Seconds the Snooze button waits before ringing again, 0 for no Snooze button or 60 to 3600. Defaults to 540 for an alarm and 0 for a timer.

params.name: snoozeLimit
params.description: How many times Snooze may be used, 1 to 10, before only Stop is offered. Needs a snooze time; leave out for no limit.

params.name: sound
params.description: default, a tone from this package (pulse or chime), or a sound file bundled with your app. File paths are not accepted.

params.name: tint
params.description: An accent colour as #RRGGBB for the alert, notification or card.

params.name: title
params.description: The title shown on the alert, the Lock Screen and the notification; defaults to Alarm, or Timer for timers.

errors.message: layout must be a component name: the <activity> document for the alarm's Live Activity.

errors.message: mission must be a component name (a letter, then letters, digits, _ or .); missionLabel needs a mission and up to 40 characters.
errors.description: The mission is not a component name or the label is too long.
errors.whatToDo: Use a component name and a label up to 40 characters.

errors.message: rearm needs a mission and is 0 or a whole number of seconds from 10 to 3600.
errors.description: Rearm needs a mission and must be 0 or 10 to 3600 seconds.
errors.whatToDo: Add a mission and use a valid number of seconds.

errors.message: A timer takes a duration, never at, time or repeats.
errors.description: The time arguments do not fit this call.
errors.whatToDo: Give exactly one of at and time for an alarm, or only a duration for a timer.

errors.message: snooze must be 0 or a whole number of seconds from 60 to 3600.
errors.description: The snooze time is not 0 or between 60 and 3600 seconds.
errors.whatToDo: Use 0 or a whole number from 60 to 3600.

errors.message: snoozeLimit is a whole number from 1 to 10 and needs a snooze.
errors.description: The snooze limit is not 1 to 10 or no snooze time is set.
errors.whatToDo: Use a whole number from 1 to 10 together with a snooze time.

errors.message: sound must be default or a bundled sound file name.
errors.description: The sound is not default or a bundled sound file name.
errors.whatToDo: Use default, pulse, chime or a file bundled with the app.

errors.message: tint must be #RRGGBB.
errors.description: The tint is not written as #RRGGBB.
errors.whatToDo: Use a six digit hex colour such as #FF3B30.

errors.message: title must be a non-empty string of at most 120 characters.
errors.description: The title is empty or longer than 120 characters.
errors.whatToDo: Give a title of 1 to 120 characters.

errors.message: The alarm grant is not given. data carries the contract state { permission, status, canAsk }: ask again while canAsk, otherwise only Settings can change it (permission.openSettings).
errors.description: The person has not allowed alarms for this app.
errors.whatToDo: If canAsk is true call permission.request, otherwise send them to Settings with permission.openSettings.

errors.message: The OS refused the alarm (AlarmKit's limit, or the exact-alarm grant was revoked).
errors.description: The system refused to create the alarm, for example at its alarm limit or because exact alarms were turned off.
errors.whatToDo: Remove an old alarm or ask the person to allow exact alarms, then try again.

errors.message: This device has no alarm service: AlarmKit needs iOS 26 (proposals/alarms.md section 6).
errors.description: This device has no alarm service, because iOS alarms need iOS 26.
errors.whatToDo: Hide the alarm feature or use a notification instead on older devices.

packages.title: Sign in with Apple
packages.summary: Let people sign in to your app with their Apple ID.
packages.description: Shows Apple's native sign-in sheet and returns an ID token, authorization code, email and name for your account service to verify. The build turns on the Sign in with Apple entitlement for you. Needs an Apple Developer account with Sign in with Apple enabled on your app ID. iOS only.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it when you want a one-tap Apple sign-in on iOS that gives your account service an identity token to verify. It is the right choice for any iOS app that also offers other social sign-ins, since the App Store expects Apple as an option.

actions.description: Shows Apple's native sign-in sheet and returns the identity token, authorization code, nonce, Apple user id and, on the first sign-in only, the person's name and email.

actions.whenNotToUse: Do not use it to read a name or email again later, since Apple sends them only the first time.

params.name: nonce
params.description: A random value your backend minted to tie this sign-in to a request. Leave it out and one is created for you.

result.description: The person's email, sent only on the first authorization and empty afterwards.

result.name: familyName
result.description: The person's last name, sent only on the first authorization and empty afterwards.

result.name: givenName
result.description: The person's first name, sent only on the first authorization and empty afterwards.

result.name: idToken
result.description: The signed token to send to whatever verifies the sign-in. If it is missing the sign-in was refused.

result.name: nonce
result.description: The raw nonce, which a verifier hashes and compares with the one inside the token.

result.name: realUserStatus
result.description: Apple's own signal about whether this is a real person: likelyReal, unknown or unsupported.

result.name: userIdentifier
result.description: Apple's stable id for this person in your app. Store it, since it is the one field that always arrives.

packages.whenToUse: Use it after a moment when the user is likely to be happy, such as finishing a task. Do not attach it to a button labelled rate us, because the system may show nothing; link to your store page for that.
packages.nativeValue: The system sheet lets people leave a rating in one tap without going to the store, and the platforms keep it from being shown too often.

actions.name: request

actions.whenNotToUse: Do not call it from a rate-us button, since the system may show nothing.

result.name: requested
result.description: True when the system was asked to show the sheet; false when it could not be asked, for example when no screen was in front.

packages.title: AppsFlyer
packages.summary: Attribute installs and purchases to ad campaigns with AppsFlyer.
packages.description: Starts the AppsFlyer SDK at launch, logs in-app events and ad revenue, reports where an install came from and resolves OneLink deep links into your app. Does nothing until a dev key is set. Needs an AppsFlyer account, your dev key and, on iOS, your Apple app ID.

packages.title: AppTracking
packages.summary: Ask the user for tracking permission and read their answer.
packages.description: Lets your app find out whether the user allows tracking and ask for it when you choose. On iOS it shows Apple's App Tracking Transparency dialog; on Android it reports the Google Play advertising ID opt-out. The framework never asks on launch, so you decide when to call it. You write the screen that explains why you ask and the code that turns tracking or personalised ads off.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when your app has cross-app tracking, personalised ads or attribution that depends on user consent, and you need to show the iOS tracking dialog at the right moment. Skip it if your app does no tracking, since nothing asks on launch.

packages.title: Firebase Auth
packages.summary: Sign people in with Firebase Authentication using email and password, Google or Apple.
packages.description: Keeps accounts in your Firebase project and signs people in with email and password, or with a Google or Apple credential. Gives you the Firebase ID token to check on your own server. Use it if your accounts already live in Firebase. Needs a Firebase project and its Web API key.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it when your accounts already live in a Firebase project and you want email and password, Google or Apple sign-in. It does not offer emailed codes, phone codes or passkeys, so use another sign-in package for those.

config.label: Firebase Web API key
config.description: Your Firebase project's Web API key (Project settings, General). It starts with AIza.

config.label: Auth emulator or proxy
config.description: Leave blank for Firebase. For the local Auth emulator use http://127.0.0.1:9099 (http://10.0.2.2:9099 from the Android emulator).

packages.title: Despia Identity
packages.summary: Sign people in with emailed codes using your own self-hosted identity service.
packages.description: Emails a one-time code, checks it and keeps the person signed in, with no third-party account service. Use it when you want to own your user accounts. Needs the open Despia identity service deployed and its address.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it when you want emailed one-time codes and to host your own accounts with the open identity service. If your accounts live in another service such as Firebase, Supabase or Clerk, use that package instead.

config.label: Identity service
config.description: The address of your identity service deployment (OpenSource/Services/identity), for example https://id.example.com.

packages.title: Automotive
packages.summary: Run your app on cars that have Android built in, using Android Automotive OS.
packages.description: Adds Android Automotive OS support to the Car package. Cars with Android built in need their own app build, and this package makes that build: you export for the automotive track and the car launches your car templates directly. Include it only in the build you ship to the automotive track, since a phone build that contains it is refused. Android only.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when you ship a car app to the Android Automotive track on Google Play, for cars that run Android themselves. Skip it for phone projection through Android Auto or CarPlay, which the Car package already covers.

actions.name: status

result.description: True when the device is a car that runs Android Automotive OS, false on phones and emulators.

result.name: templatesHost
result.description: True when the device has the host that shows car app templates, which the car screens need.

packages.summary: Let devices upload files straight to your own storage bucket with short-lived signed links.

packages.title: Backend
packages.summary: Server-side half of device integrity: reads and writes per-device flags that survive reinstalls.
packages.description: Runs on your own server and talks to Apple DeviceCheck and Google Play Integrity. It checks a device claim sent by your app, then reads or writes a few flags tied to that physical device, such as "this device already used its free trial". Your keys stay on your server, and you decide what each flag means.
packages.whenToUse: Use it on your server to stop one device from claiming a free trial or promotion again after reinstalling. It should gate a benefit, never a sign-in.

actions.name: recall
actions.description: Reads the per-device flags for a device claim, and optionally writes them first. It checks the claim with Apple or Google before answering.
actions.whenNotToUse: Do not call it from the app, since a device that could call it could clear its own flags. Call it only from your own server code.

params.name: challenge
params.description: The one-time challenge your server issued for this claim.

params.name: format
params.description: Which service made the claim: apple.devicecheck or google.playintegrity.

params.name: set
params.description: Values to write first, one entry per flag: true or false to write it, null to leave it alone.

params.name: token
params.description: The token the device produced, as sent by your app.

result.name: bits
result.description: The flags after any write: two on Apple and three on Google.

result.name: format
result.description: The claim format that was checked.

result.name: known
result.description: False for a device your app never wrote to, in which case every flag is false.

result.name: months
result.description: When each flag was last changed as YYYY-MM, or empty while it is unset.

result.name: provider
result.description: The service that answered, Apple or Google.

errors.message: The Play Integrity token does not prove this claim; data.why names it: wrong_app (made for another package), challenge_mismatch (made for another challenge), stale_token (older than ten minutes).
errors.description: The Play Integrity token does not prove this claim; data.why says it was made for another app or challenge, or is older than ten minutes.
errors.whatToDo: Ask the app for a fresh claim with your current challenge.

errors.message: The request cannot be acted on; data.why names it: missing (token or challenge), unknown_format (not apple.devicecheck or google.playintegrity), set (not a list of true, false or null within the provider's bits, or changing nothing), invalid_token (Apple or Google could not read the device's token).
errors.description: The request cannot be acted on; data.why says whether the token or challenge is missing, the format is unknown, set is invalid or the token is unreadable.
errors.whatToDo: Check the value named in data.why and send a corrected request.

errors.message: data.why names it: setup (the DeviceCheck key, key ID, team ID or environment, or the Play Integrity service account or package name, is missing or malformed; data.what names the setting), recall_unavailable (the verdict carries no device recall: the app is not enrolled in Play Integrity device recall, or the account is not licensed).
errors.description: The server is missing setup for this service; data.why says whether a key setting is missing or Play Integrity device recall is not enabled.
errors.whatToDo: Add the missing setting named in data.what, or enrol the app in device recall in the Play Console.

errors.message: Apple or Google did not answer usefully; data.why names it: rate_limited, provider_down, unexpected_reply. Try again later.
errors.description: Apple or Google did not answer usefully; data.why says whether it was rate limiting, an outage or an unexpected reply.
errors.whatToDo: Try again later.

errors.message: Apple or Google refused the request (data.why provider_refused, data.vendorCode its HTTP status): an unknown key, an expired authentication token, a forbidden action.
errors.description: Apple or Google refused the request, for example because of an unknown key or an expired authentication token.
errors.whatToDo: Check the keys and settings on your server, using data.vendorCode for the status.

packages.title: Background
packages.summary: Runs your app's declared tasks in the background and tells you honestly when they ran.
packages.description: Lets you declare periodic, one-time and refresh tasks and ask the system to run them while the app is closed. Neither iOS nor Android promises exact timing, so the status report shows when each task really ran, how long it took, how it ended and why it has not run yet. You write the action each task calls.
packages.whenToUse: Use it for work that can wait and does not need exact timing, such as syncing data, uploading a queue or warming content. Do not use it for anything that must happen at a fixed time, which needs a scheduled notification or a server.

packages.title: Base
packages.summary: A private on-device database for your app's own data, with documents, queries, backups and vector search.
packages.description: Gives the app one local database file holding key and value documents, queries over them, savepoints you can roll back, durable snapshots and a vector index for similarity search. Live queries keep a list in your screens up to date as data changes. You decide the stores and the shape of your data; nothing is sent off the device.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when the app needs to store and search its own data on the device, offline and fast, including notes, caches, drafts or embeddings for search. Do not use it for data that must be shared between users; that belongs on your backend.
packages.nativeValue: A real on-device database is faster, works offline and survives restarts, which browser storage cannot promise, and it can keep durable backups.

packages.title: Face ID and Touch ID
packages.summary: Confirm it is really the user with Face ID, Touch ID or the device passcode.
packages.description: Shows the system prompt so the user can confirm it is them with biometrics, falling back to the device passcode. Without a challenge the answer is a yes or no for the interface (a modified client can fake it, so it never protects data); pass a server challenge and the answer is a passkey assertion your server verifies. To keep a secret behind biometrics use the vault's locked records. You write the reason text shown in the prompt.
packages.whenToUse: Use it to confirm the person holding the phone before showing a screen or acting on a tap. For anything that protects data or money, pass a server challenge so your server can verify the answer.
packages.nativeValue: Face ID, Touch ID and the Android fingerprint prompt use the secure hardware and the system's own sheet, which a web page cannot reach.

actions.name: authenticate

actions.whenToUse: Use it to unlock a screen or confirm a sensitive tap. Add a challenge when your server must be able to trust the answer.
actions.whenNotToUse: Without a challenge, do not rely on it to protect data, money or a sign-in, because a modified app could fake the yes.

packages.title: Block editor
packages.summary: Add a Notion-style editor where people write notes and documents in blocks.

packages.title: Bluetooth
packages.summary: Connect your app to nearby Bluetooth Low Energy devices.
packages.description: Scans for Bluetooth Low Energy devices, connects, discovers services and reads, writes and subscribes to their data. Use it for wearables, sensors and other accessories. Asks for Bluetooth permission the first time it is used, with text you set. Works on phones and desktop.
packages.whenToUse: Use it to talk to Bluetooth Low Energy accessories such as heart rate straps, sensors and smart devices. It does not handle classic Bluetooth audio or pairing screens.
packages.nativeValue: Native Bluetooth scans passively, keeps connections and notifications running in the background, and replays what you missed, which Web Bluetooth cannot.

actions.name: connect
actions.description: Connects to a device found by scanning, waiting for the radio to be on if needed, and reports the negotiated MTU (null on the web).

params.name: autoConnect
params.description: Pass true to reconnect automatically after an unexpected drop; an explicit disconnect turns it off. Defaults to false. Has no effect on the web.

params.name: deviceId
params.description: The device id from a device event while scanning; opaque and platform specific (a per-app UUID on iOS that can change after a reinstall, the Bluetooth address on Android, a browser-issued id on the web).

params.name: server
params.description: An https address that receives a copy of connection events for your backend.

params.name: timeout
params.description: How long to wait for the connection, in milliseconds, before giving up. Defaults to 10000.

result.name: deviceId
result.description: The deviceId of the connected device.

result.name: mtu
result.description: The negotiated ATT MTU in bytes, so a write without response can carry up to mtu - 3 bytes. Android requests 517 after connecting; iOS reports the maximum write-without-response length plus 3. Always null on the web, which has no MTU API.

result.name: state
result.description: The connection state, connected on success.

actions.name: scan
actions.description: Scans for nearby Bluetooth Low Energy devices and sends a device event (with its deviceId) for each one found, until the duration ends or you stop it. On the web, where the browser only offers a device chooser, allowDuplicates and rssiThreshold are ignored and one device event fires for the pick.
actions.whenToUse: Use it to let the user choose a nearby accessory.

params.name: allowDuplicates
params.description: Pass true to report a device again on every advertisement, which you need for a live signal-strength meter. Defaults to false (each device once per scan). Ignored on the web chooser.

params.name: duration
params.description: How long to scan, in milliseconds. Defaults to 10000.

params.name: rssiThreshold
params.description: Signal strength floor in dBm, for example -80; devices weaker than this are not reported. Ignored on the web chooser.

params.name: scanMode
params.description: How aggressively to scan: lowLatency (default), balanced or lowPower. Android only; ignored on iOS and the web.

params.name: services
params.description: Only report devices that advertise these service UUIDs, as a list; filtering by service is more reliable than by name.

result.name: ended
result.description: True when the scan finished.

packages.title: ScreenBrightness
packages.summary: Raise or lower the screen brightness and put it back afterwards.
packages.description: Sets the screen brightness from 0 to 1, reads it, and restores the level the person had before. The original level is remembered the first time you set it and is put back automatically when the app goes to the background, so your change never outlives the app. No permission is needed. You decide when to brighten the screen.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when the screen must be bright for a moment, for example to show a barcode or a QR code to a scanner. Always restore when you are done, and do not use it to dim the screen to save power.
packages.nativeValue: It changes the real screen brightness, which a web page is not allowed to do.

packages.title: Calls
packages.summary: Add voice and video calls that ring like real phone calls.
packages.description: Handles incoming and outgoing calls with the phone's own call screen, ringing, picture in picture and audio routing, plus ready-made call screens. It needs a call provider package (Despia, LiveKit, Twilio or Stream) to carry the audio and video.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it when your app needs voice or video calls that ring and show up like real phone calls, with the lock screen call screen, picture in picture and audio routing. It carries no audio or video itself, so you also need a call provider package.

packages.title: Despia Calls
packages.summary: Carry your app's calls over WebRTC through your own Despia Calls service.
packages.description: Works with the Calls package. One-to-one calls go peer to peer, and group calls go through a media server your service names. Needs the Despia Calls service deployed, plus a token endpoint on your back end.
packages.whenToUse: Use it as the call engine when you run your own Despia Calls service and want one-to-one calls to go directly between devices. You still use the calls package for the commands.

config.label: Calls service
config.description: The address of your Despia Calls service (OpenSource/Services/calls), which carries the call's signalling.

config.label: Join token endpoint
config.description: Your own back end's endpoint that answers { token, peer } for the signed in user and a call id: GET <tokenUrl>?callId=<id>.

packages.title: LiveKit Calls
packages.summary: Run your app's calls and group rooms on LiveKit.
packages.description: Works with the Calls package. Joins LiveKit rooms, shares microphone and camera and shows everyone's video. Needs a LiveKit server and an endpoint on your back end that issues join tokens.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it when you want your calls and group rooms to run on LiveKit. It needs the call package, a LiveKit server and a way to get a join token for each person.

actions.name: session
actions.description: Gives the LiveKit provider the join token and server address for the next call, and reports whether it is ready.
actions.whenToUse: Call it with a token from your server just before you start or answer a call.
actions.whenNotToUse: Never create tokens on the device; get them from your server.

params.name: token
params.description: The join token for this person and room, made by your server.

params.name: url

result.name: ready
result.description: True when the provider holds a token and server address and can join.

errors.whatToDo: Pass a token and a server address, or set the token endpoint and server address in the package settings.

config.label: LiveKit server url
config.description: The websocket url of your LiveKit server or LiveKit Cloud project (wss://<project>.livekit.cloud). Takes {{ }}.

packages.title: Twilio Voice
packages.summary: Make and receive voice calls with Twilio.
packages.description: Works with the Calls package. Places calls to Twilio clients and receives incoming calls on the phone's call screen. Needs a Twilio account and a server that issues Twilio access tokens. Voice only, on iOS, Android and the web.
packages.whenToUse: Use it with the Calls package when your voice calls run on Twilio. Your server must mint Twilio access tokens; this package never needs your Auth Token or API secret.
packages.nativeValue: Incoming calls ring on the phone's native call screen even when the app is closed, which a web page cannot do.

packages.title: Camera burst
packages.summary: Capture photos from the camera in code, with no preview screen.
packages.description: Takes a set number of photos as fast as the hardware allows and returns them as files, with no preview or shutter button. Use it when your app captures frames alongside a sensor reading or other event. Asks for camera permission the first time it runs. Phones only.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it when your app needs the camera in code: a burst of photos matched to a sensor reading, a held-open session with controls and recording, or a live preview you draw yourself. For a picker where the person chooses a photo, use the platform file picker instead.
packages.nativeValue: Uses the real camera pipelines (AVFoundation, CameraX) for low-latency capture, HDR, ProRes, RAW and lens control that a web page cannot reach.

actions.name: burst
actions.description: Takes a number of photos in a row as fast as the hardware allows, with no preview, and returns them as files.
actions.whenToUse: Use it to capture frames alongside a sensor reading or another event.
actions.whenNotToUse: Do not use it for a camera screen the person looks at; use a session with a preview instead.

params.name: camera
params.description: Which camera to use: back or front.

params.name: count
params.description: How many photos to take, from 1 up to the configured maximum burst length.

params.name: interval
params.description: Minimum milliseconds between photos; 0 means as fast as the sensor delivers.

params.name: prompt
params.description: Set false to never show the permission dialog; the call then fails with permission_denied instead.

params.name: quality
params.description: JPEG quality from 0.01 to 1; the default is 0.9.

result.name: count
result.description: How many photos were really captured; compare it with what you asked for.

result.name: durationMs
result.description: How long the burst itself took in milliseconds, not counting camera warm-up.

result.name: photos
result.description: The photos in capture order, each with a Files path, size, byte count and timestamp.

errors.message: A burst is already running.
errors.description: Another capture is already using the camera.
errors.whatToDo: Wait for the running capture to finish, and disable your shutter control while context.capturing or a session is active.

errors.message: The capture session could not be started.
errors.description: The camera session or the output folder could not be set up, or the capture itself failed.
errors.whatToDo: Try again; if it keeps failing, check that another app is not holding the camera and that the device has free storage.

errors.message: Camera access is not granted. The data carries the contract state: { permission, status, canAsk }.
errors.description: The camera permission is not granted, so nothing was captured.
errors.whatToDo: Read data.canAsk: if true call permission.request first, otherwise show a row that opens Settings.

errors.description: There is no camera, or none on the side you asked for.
errors.whatToDo: Check dsx.has before offering the feature, and hide the control on devices without a camera.

errors.message: This device has no camera to take a burst with.

packages.title: Capture
packages.summary: Turn any element or screen into an image, a PDF or a screen recording.
packages.description: Takes a picture of one named element, the whole app window or a component that was never shown, and writes it as a PNG, JPEG or WebP file in your app's storage. packages.title: Car
packages.summary: Show lists, grids and messages on the car's screen with CarPlay and Android Auto.
packages.description: Takes a short car layout from your app and shows it on the vehicle's own dashboard using the templates that CarPlay and Android Auto allow: lists, grids, panes, messages and tab bars. Taps on rows come back to your app as events. Apple must grant the CarPlay entitlement for your app category before it works on a real car. You write the layout and handle the taps.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when your app fits a car app category such as audio, messaging or navigation and you want a simple list-based screen in the car. It cannot show custom drawings or web pages, because cars only allow their fixed templates.
packages.nativeValue: The car system itself draws the templates, so they follow the vehicle's design and driving safety rules, which an app cannot bypass.

packages.title: Chat
packages.summary: Add messaging to your app with conversations, replies, attachments and typing.
packages.description: Gives your app conversation lists, message sending that shows at once and delivers when online, read receipts, typing indicators and attachments. It needs a chat provider package (Despia, Stream or Sendbird) to carry the messages.
packages.whenToUse: Use it to add conversations, direct messages or an assistant chat to your app, with messages that show at once and send when the device is online. It needs a chat provider package to carry the messages, and it does not draw the screens by itself.
packages.nativeValue: Messages are stored on the device and sent from an outbox, so the chat keeps working offline and survives the app being closed.

packages.title: Encrypted chat
packages.summary: Make chat messages end-to-end encrypted so only the people in the conversation can read them.
packages.description: Works with the Chat package. Encrypts each message on the sender's device and decrypts it on the others using the MLS standard, so the server never sees the text. Use it for private conversations. Needs the Chat package.

packages.title: Sendbird Chat

packages.title: Stream Chat
packages.summary: Run your app's chat on Stream.
packages.description:
Works with the Chat package. Carries messages live through your Stream app on the web, iOS and Android. Needs a Stream account, your API key and a token endpoint on your server.

![A conversation drawn by the Chat package's bubbles, carried by Stream](media/chat.png)

## What moves live

Stream's SDK keeps a connection open, so new messages, reactions, read and delivery state and the other person's typing arrive as Stream sends them. A reaction, an edit and a delete are Stream's own, and a reply is a Stream thread reply that also shows in the channel.

## Set it up

1. Create an app in the [Stream dashboard](https://getstream.io/chat/) and copy its API key and secret.
2. Add **Stream Chat** to your app. Its server half answers `POST /stream/token` for the signed-in user, so the secret never reaches the device.
3. Set `STREAM_API_KEY` and `STREAM_SECRET_KEY` as secrets of your server.
4. Open a conversation from the Chat package's screen. A conversation id is Stream's channel id, such as `messaging:general`.

## What it adds

| Target | Library | Version |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Web | stream-chat | 9.53.0 |
| iOS | StreamChat (Swift Package Manager) | 5.12.0 |
| Android | stream-chat-android-client | 7.12.0 |
packages.whenToUse: Use it when you want the Chat package to run on your own Stream Chat account, with live messages, reactions and typing. Skip it if you use the default chat provider or another vendor.

packages.title: Clipboard
packages.summary: Read from and write to the system clipboard, with a way to peek without triggering the paste alert.
packages.description: Gives you one call to read text, links, rich text, images and files from the clipboard, one to write them with options such as expiry and sensitive content, and one to check what is there without reading it. A change notification tells you when the clipboard changes. You write the buttons and screens that use it.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it for copy buttons, paste buttons and share-to-clipboard features. For plain copy of a short string on a web page the browser clipboard may be enough, but this also handles images and expiry.
packages.nativeValue: Checking what is on the clipboard first avoids the system paste alert on iOS and Android, which web pages cannot do.

packages.title: Despia Commerce
packages.summary: Verify purchases and keep entitlements on your own server, with no third party in between.
packages.description: Sends every App Store and Google Play purchase to your own Despia Commerce deployment, which verifies the store's signature and keeps the entitlements. packages.title: Stripe Connect

packages.description: Adds Stripe's own Connect components to your layout or as sheets, such as onboarding, payments and payouts, so sellers or providers on your platform manage their money without leaving the app. Works with the Stripe package. packages.title: Image safety check
packages.summary: Detect explicit images on the device so your content rules can hold or block them.
packages.description: Checks photos for explicit or suggestive content and passes the result to the Content policy package, which decides what to do. The image never leaves the device. On iOS it uses Apple's own detector, which respects the Sensitive Content Warning setting. Works with the Content policy package.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when your app lets people share photos and you want explicit images flagged on the device, before sending or after receiving. It only produces a score, and your content rules decide what happens next.
packages.nativeValue: Detection runs on the device, so the photo never leaves it, and on Apple devices it uses the system's own detector and the person's Sensitive Content Warning setting.

packages.title: Converse
packages.summary: Hold a spoken conversation with an AI model entirely on the device, with no network.
packages.description: Runs a voice call loop: it listens to the person, turns speech into text, asks a local language model for an answer and speaks the reply, one turn at a time. The person can interrupt the reply by talking over it. It works on top of the on-device AI and voice packages, which must be included. You choose the models and write the call screen.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it for a private voice assistant or concierge that must work offline. It is not shipped yet and needs the on-device AI package, a speech model, a language model and a voice. Only one call can run at a time.
packages.nativeValue: Everything stays on the phone, so the conversation works offline and nothing is sent to a server.

packages.title: Crypto
packages.summary: Hash, sign, encrypt and generate random values with the phone's own crypto.
packages.description: Gives you digests, HMAC, secure random numbers and UUIDs (v4 and time-sortable v7), plus Ed25519 and P-256 signing and AES-256-GCM encryption. Keys are created and kept in the secure store, in secure hardware when the device has it, and you only ever hold a reference. The package uses each platform's own implementation and adds no crypto of its own.
packages.whenToUse: Use it to hash or sign data, make unique ids, draw fair random numbers or encrypt small values with a key the device protects. For storing a secret between launches, use the secure storage package instead.
packages.nativeValue: Keys can live in the Secure Enclave or StrongBox and never leave the device, which a web page cannot guarantee.

packages.title: Data
packages.summary: Declare the data tables your packages need, once, for any database you choose.
packages.description: Lets a package declare its own entities with named fields, indexes and an ownership rule, and compiles them for whichever database the build uses. Field types come from a small fixed list so the same declaration works everywhere. This package defines the schema word only; nothing in an app calls it at runtime, and you write the entities in the packages that need them.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when you author a server package that stores its own records and want them created in the configured database without writing SQL or security rules. App builders who only use finished packages never need to touch it.

packages.title: Device
packages.summary: Read the device, the app's own identity, the screen, locale, battery and display capabilities.
packages.description: Gives you plain answers about the phone or tablet the app runs on: hardware and OS, the app's version and first-launch state, screen size with real safe-area insets, language and region, battery and thermal state, and which hardware features exist. It needs no permission and never polls. You decide how your screens adapt to the answers.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it when a screen must adapt to the device: safe-area padding, a first-launch welcome, a what's-new sheet, lighter effects on old or hot hardware, or locale-aware formatting. It does not tell you whether the user granted a permission; use the package that owns that feature.

packages.title: DeviceUsage
packages.summary: Block chosen apps and websites for a set time, on a daily schedule, or after a daily limit is used up.
packages.description: Lets the person pick apps to block, then blocks them now for a set time, every day in a time window, or once a daily limit is reached. It uses Screen Time on iOS and a blocking service on Android, with the same calls on both. You get the picker, the rules and the block screen, and you write the screens that explain why.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it for focus, digital wellbeing or parental-style features where your app limits other apps. Do not use it to limit your own app, and note that it needs special system permissions the person must grant.
packages.nativeValue: The operating system enforces the blocks even when your app is closed on iOS, which a web page cannot do at all.

packages.title: Dom
packages.summary: Control the web view that shows your web app: load pages, navigate, run scripts.
packages.description: Gives you the remote control for the web view that displays your site inside the app: load a page or a bundled file, go back and forward, reload, recover after a crash, run a script, add scripts that run on every page, manage cookies and clear web data. It ships with every app and drives the web view you place in your layout. You write the pages and the calls.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when your layout shows a web view and you need to steer it from buttons or code. Do not use it to pass data to new features; publish state on a package context and broadcast events instead of writing page globals.
packages.nativeValue: It drives the real WKWebView or Android WebView, so back and forward, crash recovery, cookie handling and script injection behave like a native browser host.

packages.title: Handoff
packages.summary: Let people start in your app on an iPhone and continue on a Mac or iPad.
packages.description: Advertises what the person is doing so a nearby Apple device offers to pick it up, with a web address as a fallback for devices without your app. It checks the activity type and payload size for you, because Apple fails silently when either is wrong. You decide the activity types and what small identifiers to hand over.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when a task, such as reading a recipe or editing a note, makes sense to continue on another Apple device. Hand over an identifier and fetch the rest on the other side; do not try to pass whole documents.

packages.title: IdentityVault
packages.summary: Stores small secrets on the device in the system keychain, with an optional Face ID or fingerprint lock.
packages.description: Writes and reads small pieces of text, such as an anonymous user id or a token, in the secure store of the device. Records can be locked so they release only after Face ID, Touch ID or the passcode, and can follow the user to a new phone through iCloud Keychain or Google Block Store. It also reports honestly how long a record will last.
packages.whenToUse: Use it for small secrets that must survive reinstalls or follow the user, such as an anonymous identity behind a purchase. Do not use it for large data or ordinary settings.

packages.title: Import
packages.summary: Use an npm package from your backend code.
packages.description: Lets backend code call a real library, such as a payment SDK, without writing an import statement. You pin the npm package in the same manifest and give it a name, and your code reaches every export of it through that name. It applies to the server side only. You write the calls and handle their results.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when your backend logic needs a published npm library such as a payment or email SDK. Skip it if built-in data, queue and secret features cover the job.

packages.title: App integrity check
packages.summary: Prove to your server that a request comes from a genuine, unmodified copy of your app.
packages.description: Uses Apple App Attest on iOS and Google Play Integrity on Android to produce a token your backend verifies with Apple or Google. Use it to protect your API from fake or tampered apps. Needs a server that checks the token. For iOS you pick the development or production environment in the settings.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it to protect your own API from fake or tampered copies of your app: your server sends a challenge, the app returns a token, and your server checks it with Apple or Google. Do not use it to decide things inside the app, since a check run on the device can be patched.
packages.nativeValue: The token comes from Apple App Attest or Google Play Integrity, so the trust rests with Apple or Google and not with code on the device.

packages.title: On-device AI
packages.summary: Run a language model and speech-to-text directly on the user's device, with no server.
packages.description: Chat with a small language model, transcribe speech from a file or the microphone, detect language and search by meaning, all on the device. Models are downloaded once from approved hosts, and you can add your own. Not yet shipped: some actions are still missing, so check before relying on it.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it for private, offline chat, dictation or search by meaning where the data should stay on the device. Do not rely on it yet: it is not shipped and some actions are still absent. Models are large downloads, so check the device first.
packages.nativeValue: The model runs on the phone's own processor and memory, so it works offline and the text never leaves the device.

config.label: Allowed model hosts
config.description: Hosts this app may download AI models from, https only. The shipped catalog's models live on huggingface.co, so those hosts are here already and downloads work out of the box. Add your own host to serve your own models, for example models.yourcompany.com, or *.yourcompany.com for its subdomains. Empty this list and nothing downloads at all.

config.label: Model memory budget
config.description: How much of the memory this app still has left may be held by loaded AI models at once, as a percentage. At the default 70, loading a model that would push the total past 70% of what the app has left unloads the least recently used model first, so the rest stays free for your screens, images and the next model's load. Raise it toward 100 to keep more models loaded at the same time and leave the app less room for everything else. Set it to 0 for no limit: models are never unloaded automatically, which is the right answer on a desktop or a dedicated device with memory to spare, and a way to get the app killed on a phone.

config.label: Model registries
config.description: Where despia.intelligence.models.add may look up a model, as URL templates. Hugging Face is here already, so models.add({ source: "hf:org/repo/file.gguf" }) works out of the box. Add your own registry to resolve your own models, where the key is the source prefix your app writes. Empty this and models.add resolves nothing.

packages.title: Intents
packages.summary: Open Android system screens and other apps by intent, and check which apps can handle one.
packages.description: Lets your app launch Android intents, which reach system settings pages that have no web address, hand a file to one specific app, or trigger a phone maker feature. It can also list the apps that could handle an intent and tell you whether any can. It does nothing on iOS or the web.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it on Android when you need a settings page such as your app's own details screen, or want to hand something to a named app. For ordinary web links use the external apps package instead.
packages.nativeValue: Intents are Android's own way to reach settings pages and other apps, and a web page has no way to start them.

packages.title: Intercom
packages.summary: Add Intercom's Messenger so users can chat with support, read help articles and track tickets.
packages.description: Identifies the signed-in person to Intercom, keeps their name, email and custom details current, and opens the Messenger on home, messages, help or tickets. You can also show the unread count. Needs an Intercom account, your App ID and the iOS and Android API keys, plus a server-made identity hash. iOS and Android only.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when your support team answers customers in Intercom and you want its Messenger inside your app. If you only need a simple contact form, you do not need it.

packages.title: Stripe Issuing
packages.summary: Let people add your Stripe-issued cards to Apple Wallet or Google Wallet.
packages.description: Adds an Add to Wallet button that only shows when the card and the device can take it, and shows the card number safely on the web inside Stripe's own display. packages.title: KeepAwake
packages.summary: Keep the screen from dimming or locking while something on screen needs to stay visible.

packages.title: Kiosk
packages.summary: Lock an Android device to your app so people cannot leave it, for shared or public devices.
packages.description: Turns a company-owned Android device into a kiosk: it keeps people in your app and any other apps you allow, and can hide the status bar, the lock screen and some system buttons. packages.title: V3 compatibility
packages.summary: Keep the old window.despia calls from your V3 app working after you move to V4.
packages.description: V3 pages talk to the native app with calls like window.despia = "lighthaptic://" and read old global variables and callbacks. This package catches those calls and runs them through the current packages, so your existing pages keep working without edits. Add it when moving a V3 app, and drop it once your pages use the new calls. It only covers features the other packages in your app provide.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it when you are moving a V3 app to V4 and your pages still call window.despia with old spellings such as lighthaptic:// or read old globals. Leave it out of new apps, and drop it once your pages use the current calls.

packages.summary: Check your app's license on launch and show a blocking screen if it was revoked.
packages.description: Asks your own license server whether the app's license is still valid each time it starts, and shows a full-screen notice if it was revoked. packages.title: LightSensor
packages.summary: Read the ambient light level around the device, in lux and in simple words like dark or sunlight.
packages.description: Reports how bright the room is, either once or as a stream that only changes when the light really changes. Each reading comes with a plain category such as dark, indoor or sunlight, so you can dim a reader or brighten a screen without choosing your own thresholds. It works on Android; iOS has no public light sensor.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it to adapt your screen to the room, for example a night theme or a brighter display in sun. It does not work on iOS, so keep a manual choice for those people.
packages.nativeValue: It reads the phone's own light sensor, which a web page cannot do.

packages.title: Live Activities
packages.summary: Show live progress on the iPhone Lock Screen and Dynamic Island, and as ongoing notifications on Android.
packages.description: Start, update and end a live activity from your page, for things like a download, a delivery or a timer. On iPhone it appears on the Lock Screen and in the Dynamic Island, and on Android it shows as an ongoing notification. You design the layout as part of your app.
packages.whenToUse: Use it for something that unfolds over minutes or hours and that people want to glance at without opening the app, such as a delivery, a download, a timer or a ride. Do not make it the only way progress is shown.

packages.title: Mapbox
packages.summary: Draw your app's maps with Mapbox styles and tiles.
packages.description: Makes the Maps package draw through the Mapbox Maps SDK, so you can use Mapbox styles. Needs a Mapbox account and your public access token. Without a token the app falls back to the system map. Works with the Maps package.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it when you want your maps drawn with Mapbox styles instead of the system map. It has no calls of its own; you choose Mapbox in the Maps settings and add your public token. Without a token the system map is used.
packages.nativeValue: Maps are drawn by the Mapbox native SDK on iOS and Android, so they pan and zoom smoothly with your Mapbox styles.

packages.title: MapLibre
packages.summary: Draw your app's maps with the open source MapLibre renderer.
packages.description: Makes the Maps package draw through MapLibre instead of the system map. Needs no key or account and defaults to free public map tiles. You can point it at any MapLibre style, such as a self-hosted or Protomaps style. Works with the Maps package.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when you want maps that need no API key or vendor account, or when you want to draw your own style, such as a self-hosted or Protomaps one. Skip it if you need routes, regions, circles or the user location layer, which stay with the system map for now.

packages.title: Math formulas
packages.summary: Show math formulas, written in TeX, as properly typeset equations in your app.
packages.description: Draws formulas in markdown text, inline with $...$ or as a centred block with $$, as real typeset math instead of raw TeX source. Use it for study, science or finance content. On iOS it adds the SwiftMath typesetter and about 7 MB of math fonts; the web already shows math with the browser's own layout. Android is not covered yet.

packages.title: Photos and videos
packages.summary: Let users pick, crop, save and upload photos and videos.

packages.title: MetaConversions
packages.summary: Send your app's conversion events to Meta ads from your own server.
packages.description: Takes a Growth event on your server, checks that the person agreed to attribution and sharing with Meta, hashes their contact details and sends the event to the Meta Conversions API. It answers with whether it was sent and a record of the decision. You need a Meta dataset id and an access token, and nothing can call it from a device.
packages.whenToUse: Use it to report sign-ups, purchases and other conversions to Meta for ad measurement. It only runs on your server and only sends events for people who have given consent.

packages.title: Motion sensors
packages.summary: Read accelerometer, gyroscope, steps and activity from the device.
packages.description: Streams motion sensor data at the rate you choose, and reads the barometer, step count and activity type such as walking or driving. Use it for fitness, games and gesture features. Asks for motion permission when needed, with text you set. Phones only.

packages.title: Mount
packages.summary: Places a component or a piece of markup over your screen or web page and tells you how much space it uses.
packages.description: Mounts any imported component, such as an ad banner, over a DSX screen or a web page, on the edge you choose. The package hands back the space it takes as CSS insets so your layout can make room. You write the markup or page that hosts the mount and the CSS that uses the insets.
packages.whenToUse: Use it to put a banner, bar or overlay from another package on top of a screen or web page without hand-placing it. Do not use it for normal page content, which belongs in your own layout.
packages.nativeValue: On the web, nothing can reserve safe space for a native component. This package tells the page exactly how much room to leave, so the layout stays correct.

actions.name: declare
actions.description: Mounts a component or markup under an id, or updates it if the id already exists. If it cannot be mounted, the fallback appears, or nothing, and a failed event is sent.
actions.whenNotToUse: To change only the props of something already mounted, use set.

packages.title: Push notifications
packages.summary: Receive and show push and local notifications in your app without a third-party push SDK.
packages.description: Handles the notification permission, the device token, Android channels, action buttons, badges, images, scheduled notifications and what happens when a user taps one. Use it when you want notifications built in rather than through OneSignal, Pushwoosh or Firebase. You send pushes from your own server with your own Apple push key.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it when your app needs to remind, alert or message people outside the app, from your own server or from the device itself. If you already use a push vendor, keep it and use this package only for the local side.
packages.nativeValue: Web pages cannot reliably show notifications, set a badge or keep action buttons when the app is closed. Native notifications give you the system permission flow, app-icon badges, Android channels and reply buttons.

packages.description: Opens your provider's sign-in page in the trusted system browser sheet and hands you back every value the provider sent to your redirect address, such as the code or the tokens. packages.title: OneSignal
packages.summary: Send push notifications to your app's users through OneSignal.
packages.description:
Registers the device with OneSignal, asks for notification permission and links each device to your signed-in user, so you can send pushes from the OneSignal dashboard. Use it when your team already runs its messaging on OneSignal. Needs a OneSignal account and your OneSignal App ID.

## Set it up

1. Create an app in the [OneSignal dashboard](https://onesignal.com) and add your Apple push key and Firebase project.
2. Add **OneSignal** and paste your **OneSignal App ID**.
3. Build the app. The first launch registers the device; the permission prompt shows when your app asks for it.

## Settings

| Setting | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| OneSignal App ID | Your OneSignal application ID |
| Push enabled | Turns OneSignal push on or off |
| Open deeplink in browser | Opens a tapped notification's link in Safari instead of the app |
packages.whenToUse: Add it when your team already sends push, email and text messages from OneSignal and you want devices linked to your signed-in people. If you do not use OneSignal, use the plain notifications package.
packages.nativeValue: Uses the real OneSignal SDK and the system push permission, so delivery, opt-in state and background handling are handled the native way.

packages.summary: Lock or unlock the screen orientation while the app runs.
packages.description: Lets a screen lock portrait or landscape while it is shown and return to the app's normal setting when it leaves, for example a video that goes fullscreen sideways. packages.nativeValue: Native orientation control rotates the real interface and keeps the system rotation in step, which a web page can only ask for in a few browsers.

packages.title: Passkeys
packages.summary: Sign people in with passkeys from the phone's own authenticator, with any backend.
packages.description: Create a passkey and sign in with one using the system passkey sheet on iOS, Android and the web. You get the raw response to send to your own server, which verifies it against the challenge it issued. The package does not store credentials or verify them for you. You need your own sign-in server and a domain set up for passkeys.
packages.whenToUse: Use it for passwordless sign-in when you run your own backend or use a service that accepts standard WebAuthn responses. If you already use Clerk, use its own package instead.
packages.nativeValue: The system sheet uses the person's own Face ID, fingerprint or screen lock and syncs passkeys across their devices, which a web form cannot do.

actions.name: autofill

actions.whenNotToUse: Do not use it for a button that opens the sheet directly; use get for that.

packages.title: Pay
packages.summary: Take payments with the Apple Pay and Google Pay sheet.
packages.description: Shows the native wallet sheet or a native wallet button and hands you the payment token to send to your own payment processor. The package never sees, stores or forwards the token, and it checks that your line items add up to the total. You need a payment processor, an Apple merchant id for iOS, and Google Pay gateway details for Android.
packages.whenToUse: Use it for a one-tap checkout with the wallet the customer already trusts. If you only need card entry, use the Stripe package instead.
packages.nativeValue: The wallet sheet unlocks with Face ID or a fingerprint and uses cards already saved on the device, which a web form cannot do.

packages.title: Content policy
packages.summary: Set your own rules for what users may send, and flag, hold or block anything that breaks them.

packages.title: PushRouting
packages.summary: Delivers the notification a user tapped to your app's pages once they are ready.
packages.description: When a user taps a push notification, this package holds the payload until the page has loaded, then sends it to your app as a notification event and opens any deep-link path. packages.title: Firebase Remote Config
packages.summary: Change app settings and switch features off without releasing a new version.
packages.description: Fetches values from Firebase Remote Config, caches them and lets your screens react to them, so you can turn off a broken feature or stage a rollout. You set safe default values for when the device is offline. Needs your Firebase project set up in the app.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it to switch off a broken feature, stage a rollout or change a banner without publishing a new build. Always set defaults first so the app behaves safely when the server cannot be reached. Do not use it for private data, since the values are not secret.
packages.nativeValue: Native listeners get changes pushed to a running app, so a switch-off can reach people already using it.

actions.name: all
actions.description: Returns every active value at once, with the time they were fetched.
actions.whenToUse: Use it for a settings or debug screen. It refuses when nothing was fetched and no defaults were set.

result.description: How many parameters there are.

result.name: fetchedAt
result.description: When the values were last fetched, in epoch milliseconds.

result.name: values
result.description: A map of every parameter name to its current value as text.

actions.name: defaults

packages.title: RemoteHosts
packages.summary: Move your app to a new domain without shipping a new app version.
packages.description: Lets the app refresh its list of web hosts from a file you control, so you can change domains without an App Store rebuild. It is off until your app settings give a refresh address, and if the fetch fails the bundled hosts stay in use. You host the file and edit it when you migrate.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when you may need to change the domain your app loads from, for example during a rebrand or a client move. If your domain will never change you can leave it out.
packages.nativeValue: The app picks up the new hosts on its next launch, which a store-reviewed native build otherwise needs a full release to do.

packages.title: RevenueCat
packages.summary: Sell subscriptions and in-app purchases with RevenueCat.
packages.description: Lets your pages start a purchase, open a RevenueCat paywall or the customer center, and read products, offerings, purchase history and what a user is entitled to. Use it when your team already manages subscriptions in RevenueCat. Needs a RevenueCat account and its iOS and Android API keys.

packages.title: RevenueCat
packages.summary: Sell subscriptions and in-app purchases with RevenueCat.
packages.description: Lets your pages start a purchase, open a RevenueCat paywall or the customer center, and read products, offerings, purchase history and what a user is entitled to. Use it when your team already manages subscriptions in RevenueCat. Needs a RevenueCat account and its iOS and Android API keys.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it when your subscriptions and in-app purchases are managed in RevenueCat and you want one call to sell, show a paywall and check what a person owns. Do not include it next to the standalone RevenueCat package, since an app uses one or the other.
packages.nativeValue: Purchases run through the real App Store and Google Play billing sheets, and the paywall and customer center are RevenueCat's own native screens.

packages.title: Rive animations
packages.summary: Add interactive Rive animations that react to your app's data and send events back.
packages.description: Adds a rive element that plays a .riv file from a link or the app bundle. Its state machine inputs can follow your app's variables, so an animated cart or onboarding figure changes as the data does, and animation events can trigger actions in your app. Use it when you need animation that responds, rather than one that only plays. Needs a .riv file made in Rive.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when you want an animated figure that reacts to your data, such as an onboarding character, an animated cart or a game-like control, and your designer works in Rive. For a plain looping graphic an image or video is simpler.
packages.nativeValue: Rive's own native runtime draws the animation at full frame rate and runs its state machine, with a matching web runtime, so the same file behaves the same everywhere.

packages.title: RudderStack
packages.summary: Send your app's analytics events to your RudderStack data plane.
packages.description: Works with the Product analytics package: it delivers the events it collects to RudderStack, so you can route them on to your other tools. Delivery onward from RudderStack is not visible to the app. Needs a RudderStack source write key and the address of your data plane, cloud or self-hosted.
packages.whenToUse: Use it when your analytics events should flow into RudderStack, either RudderStack Cloud or a data plane you host yourself. Skip it if you send events to another destination, or if you cannot give it your own data plane address.

actions.name: send
actions.description: Sends one batch of collected analytics events to your RudderStack data plane as a single request. Growth calls it for you; a successful answer means the data plane accepted the batch, not that RudderStack delivered it onward.

params.name: endpoint
params.description: The address of your RudderStack data plane, such as the https URL of your cloud or self-hosted data plane. It is required in practice, because there is no default host.

params.name: events
params.description: The batch of analytics events to deliver, in the order Growth collected them.

params.name: token
params.description: Your RudderStack source write key, 20 to 64 letters and digits.

result.name: confirmed
result.description: Always false, because a success answer only shows that your data plane received the batch.

result.name: sent
result.description: How many events were in the batch the data plane accepted.

errors.message: RudderStack could not be reached.
The RudderStack data plane URL is required and must be https, or http to a local development host.
That is not a RudderStack write key (20 to 64 letters and digits).
RudderStack refused the batch.
errors.description: The data plane refused the batch with a bad request or a too large payload answer. The batch is dropped and not retried.
errors.whatToDo: Check the write key and the event contents on your RudderStack source, and keep batches smaller if the payload is too large.

packages.title: Screenshot protection
packages.summary: Hide your app's content in screenshots and screen recordings, and find out when someone tries.
packages.description: Blanks the app in screenshots and screen recordings and tells your screens when a capture is attempted, so you can blur sensitive content or warn the person. Use it for banking, health or private content. It only works while the screen capture prevention setting in the Security package is on. On Android versions before 14 it blocks capture without the notice.
packages.whenToUse: Reach for it for banking, health or private content that should not appear in screenshots or screen recordings, or when you want to warn the person that a capture was attempted. It only works while the screen capture prevention setting in the Security package is on.
packages.nativeValue: The operating system itself hides the app in captures, which a web page cannot do.

packages.whenToUse: Reach for it when your app has content people search for, such as recipes, contacts, documents or products. Do not add private content unless the person expects it to appear in system search, and clear it on sign-out.
